claim: Diabrotica virgifera virgifera is the most damaging maize pest on the planet.
source: We demonstrate that the western corn rootworm Diabrotica virgifera virgifera, the most damaging maize pest on the planet, specifically accumulates the root-derived benzoxazinoid glucosides HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, suggesting it draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: D. virgifera specifically accumulates the root-derived benzoxazinoid glucosides HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc.
source: We demonstrate that the western corn rootworm Diabrotica virgifera virgifera, the most damaging maize pest on the planet, specifically accumulates the root-derived benzoxazinoid glucosides HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A showing BX concentrations in larvae.

claim: MBOA-Glc is produced by D. virgifera through stabilization of the benzoxazinoid breakdown product MBOA by N-glycosylation.
source: MBOA-Glc is produced by D. virgifera through stabilization of the benzoxazinoid breakdown product MBOA by N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating MBOA-Glc formation in gut extracts.

claim: D. virgifera larvae can hydrolyze HDMBOA-Glc, but not MBOA-Glc, to produce toxic MBOA upon predator attack.
source: The larvae can hydrolyze HDMBOA-Glc, but not MBOA-Glc, to produce toxic MBOA upon predator attack.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing MBOA production from HDMBOA-Glc upon mechanical disruption, and Figure 2C showing no reduction in MBOA-Glc levels.

claim: Accumulation of benzoxazinoids renders D. virgifera highly resistant to nematodes which inject and feed on entomopathogenic symbiotic bacteria.
source: Accumulation of benzoxazinoids renders D. virgifera highly resistant to nematodes which inject and feed on entomopathogenic symbiotic bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing reduced EPN infectivity on WT-fed versus bx1-fed larvae.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA reduce the growth and infectivity of both the nematodes and the bacteria.
source: While HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA reduce the growth and infectivity of both the nematodes and the bacteria, MBOA-Glc repels infective juvenile nematodes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B-D showing effects on nematode infectivity, mortality, and bacterial growth.

claim: MBOA-Glc repels infective juvenile nematodes.
source: While HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA reduce the growth and infectivity of both the nematodes and the bacteria, MBOA-Glc repels infective juvenile nematodes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing reduced nematode attraction to MBOA-Glc.

claim: Herbivores combine stabilized and reactivated plant toxins to defend themselves against a deadly symbiosis between the third and the fourth trophic level enemies.
source: Our results illustrate how herbivores combine stabilized and reactivated plant toxins to defend themselves against a deadly symbiosis between the third and the fourth trophic level enemies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing effects on both nematodes (third trophic level) and bacteria (fourth trophic level).

claim: The growth and reproduction of herbivores is constrained by both plant quality and predation by higher trophic levels.
source: The growth and reproduction of herbivores is constrained by both plant quality and predation by higher trophic levels (Hunter et al., 1997; Ode, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By ingesting and accumulating plant toxins (sequestration), herbivores may make themselves unattractive or toxic to natural enemies.
source: By ingesting and accumulating plant toxins, a phenomenon referred to as sequestration, herbivores may make themselves unattractive or toxic to natural enemies (Nishida, 2002; Petschenka and Agrawal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The transfer of plant toxins across three trophic levels is increasingly recognized as a powerful force that shapes the distribution and abundance of plants, herbivores and predators in natural and agricultural ecosystems.
source: The resulting transfer of plant toxins across three trophic levels is increasingly recognized as a powerful force that shapes the distribution and abundance of plants, herbivores and predators in natural and agricultural ecosystems (Kumar et al., 2014; Hopkins et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many plants store non-toxic forms of plant defenses (protoxins) separately from the enzymes that activate them and only form the toxins upon tissue disruption.
source: Many plants store non-toxic forms of plant defenses (so called protoxins) separately from the enzymes that activate them and only form the toxins upon tissue disruption when protoxin and activating enzyme come together (Hopkins et al., 2009; Wouters et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some sequestering herbivores have evolved the ability to phenocopy two-component defense systems by stabilizing and sequestering the protoxins and producing their own activating enzymes.
source: Some sequestering herbivores in turn have evolved the ability to phenocopy these two-component defense systems by stabilizing and sequestering the protoxins and producing their own activating enzymes to release the toxins in a controlled fashion (Jones et al., 2001; Beran et al., 2014; Zagrobelny and Møller, 2011; Kazana et al., 2007; Francis et al., 2002; Opitz and Müller, 2009; Müller et al., 2001; Pontoppidan et al., 2001; Jones et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: It remains unclear whether re-activation is required for herbivore protection and which predators are targeted.
source: It remains for instance unclear whether re-activation is required for herbivore protection and which predators are targeted (Beran et al., 2014; Zagrobelny and Møller, 2011; Kazana et al., 2007; Bridges et al., 2002; Hartmann et al., 1997; Zagrobelny et al., 2007; Pratt et al., 2008; Beran et al., 2011; Agrawal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating gaps in the literature.

claim: Plant defense metabolites taken up by herbivores may influence herbivore predators and parasitoids.
source: After being taken up by herbivores, plant defense metabolites may not only influence herbivore predators and parasitoids (Ode, 2006), but also higher trophic levels (van Nouhuys et al., 2012; Harvey et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plant defense metabolites taken up by herbivores may influence higher trophic levels beyond predators and parasitoids.
source: After being taken up by herbivores, plant defense metabolites may not only influence herbivore predators and parasitoids (Ode, 2006), but also higher trophic levels (van Nouhuys et al., 2012; Harvey et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Entomopathogenic nematodes feed on insect-killing symbiotic bacteria which they inject into their herbivore hosts.
source: Entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) for instance feed on insect-killing symbiotic bacteria which they inject into their herbivore hosts (Kaya and Gaugler, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The specific effects of sequestered plant defenses on the fourth trophic level remain unknown.
source: So far, the specific effects of sequestered plant defenses on the fourth trophic level remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge without citation, representing established understanding of the field.

claim: Very little is known about plant toxin sequestration and the prevalence of two-component defense systems in belowground herbivores.
source: In contrast to aboveground herbivores, very little is known about plant toxin sequestration and the prevalence of two-component defense systems in belowground herbivores.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge, representing established understanding of the field.

claim: Root feeders are among the most important agricultural pests.
source: Root feeders are among the most important agricultural pests and can have significant impacts on the abundance and distribution of other species, including leaf feeders (Blossey and Hunt-Joshi, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Root feeders can have significant impacts on the abundance and distribution of other species, including leaf feeders.
source: Root feeders are among the most important agricultural pests and can have significant impacts on the abundance and distribution of other species, including leaf feeders (Blossey and Hunt-Joshi, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The milkweed beetle larvae Tetraopes tetraophthalmus and T. texanus accumulate cardenolides from their host plants.
source: The two milkweed beetle larvae Tetraopes tetraophthalmus and T. texanus were recently found to accumulate cardenolides from their host plants.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding, implying citation to recent literature, though the specific citation is not provided in this sentence.

claim: Sequestered cardenolide concentrations in Tetraopes larvae did not correlate with resistance to EPNs.
source: Sequestered cardenolide concentrations did not correlate with resistance to EPNs (Ali and Agrawal, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The larvae and adults of the spotted cucumber beetle Diabrotica undecimpunctata accumulate cucurbitacin triterpenes from their host plants.
source: Furthermore, the larvae and adults of the spotted cucumber beetle Diabrotica undecimpunctata accumulate cucurbitacin triterpenes from their host plants (Tallamy et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cucurbitacins are passed on to the eggs of D. undecimpunctata and can protect the eggs against pathogenic fungi.
source: Cucurbitacins are passed on to the eggs and can protect the latter against pathogenic fungi (Tallamy et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Whether cucurbitacins protect D. undecimpunctata larvae against predators and EPNs is unclear.
source: Whether cucurbitacins protect D. undecimpunctata larvae against predators (Gould and Massey, 1984) and EPNs (Barbercheck et al., 1995) is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating uncertainty in the literature.

claim: D. virgifera larvae develop exclusively on maize roots.
source: Its larvae develop exclusively on maize roots and cause over $2 billion worth of damage every year in the United States alone (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: D. virgifera causes over $2 billion worth of damage every year in the United States alone.
source: Its larvae develop exclusively on maize roots and cause over $2 billion worth of damage every year in the United States alone (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The hemolymph of D. virgifera larvae is repellent to a wide variety of predators.
source: Earlier studies found that the hemolymph of the larvae is repellent to a wide variety of predators (Lundgren et al., 2009; Welch and Lundgren, 2014), which may contribute to the limited success of biological control programs against D. virgifera (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The repellent properties of D. virgifera hemolymph may contribute to the limited success of biological control programs against D. virgifera.
source: Earlier studies found that the hemolymph of the larvae is repellent to a wide variety of predators (Lundgren et al., 2009; Welch and Lundgren, 2014), which may contribute to the limited success of biological control programs against D. virgifera (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from cited literature.

claim: The larvae of the western corn rootworm are fully tolerant to benzoxazinoids.
source: Our own work revealed that the larvae of the western corn rootworm are fully tolerant to benzoxazinoids (BXs) (Robert et al., 2012a), a dominant class of secondary metabolites in maize that provides broad spectrum resistance against a variety of other pests and diseases (Wouters et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Benzoxazinoids are a dominant class of secondary metabolites in maize that provides broad spectrum resistance against a variety of pests and diseases.
source: Our own work revealed that the larvae of the western corn rootworm are fully tolerant to benzoxazinoids (BXs) (Robert et al., 2012a), a dominant class of secondary metabolites in maize that provides broad spectrum resistance against a variety of other pests and diseases (Wouters et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: D. virgifera larvae are attracted by BXs and use them to navigate the rhizosphere and locate the most nutritious maize roots.
source: We also found that the larvae are attracted by BXs and use them to navigate the rhizosphere and locate the most nutritious maize roots (Robert et al., 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: BXs function as classical two-component defenses, with pro-toxins stored in glycosylated form in vacuoles, activating β-glucosidases in the cytosol, and BX hydrolysis occurring upon tissue disruption.
source: BXs function as classical two-component defenses, with the pro-toxins being stored in glycosylated form in the vacuoles of maize cells, the activating β-glucosidases being present in the cytosol and BX hydrolysis occurring upon tissue disruption (Jonczyk et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: EPNs are among the major natural enemies of western corn rootworm larvae.
source: EPNs are among the major natural enemies of western corn rootworm larvae and have been proposed as promising biocontrol agents to control the pest (Kurtz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: EPNs have been proposed as promising biocontrol agents to control D. virgifera.
source: EPNs are among the major natural enemies of western corn rootworm larvae and have been proposed as promising biocontrol agents to control the pest (Kurtz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Maize-fed D. virgifera larvae accumulated significant amounts of BXs in their body.
source: Metabolite analysis revealed that maize-fed D. virgifera larvae accumulated significant amounts of BXs in their body (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The highest BX concentrations in D. virgifera were found for HDMBOA-Glc (>100 µg/g FM) and MBOA-Glc (>25 µg/g FM).
source: The highest concentrations were found for the glucosides HDMBOA-Glc (>100 µg/g FM) and MBOA-Glc (>25 µg/g FM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 1A.

claim: Two generalist root feeders D. balteata and D. undecimpunctata accumulated lower amounts of BXs compared to D. virgifera.
source: In contrast to D. virgifera, two generalist root feeders of the same genus, D. balteata and D. undecimpunctata, accumulated lower amounts of BXs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In North and Central America, maize is attacked by many different Diabrotica species.
source: In North and Central America, maize is attacked by many different Diabrotica species (Szalanski et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Only D. virgifera is fully specialized on maize and causes substantial yield losses among Diabrotica species.
source: Yet, only D. virgifera is fully specialized on maize and causes substantial yield losses (Chiang, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The specialization of D. virgifera on maize might be associated with the selective accumulation of BXs.
source: Our experiments suggest that this specialization might be associated with the selective accumulation of BXs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data showing differential BX accumulation.

claim: D. virgifera accumulates HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc predominantly in the hemolymph.
source: BX screening of different larval tissues showed that D. virgifera accumulates HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc predominantly in the hemolymph (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc were detected on the exoskeleton of D. virgifera with estimated release rates of 3–6 ng/hr per larva.
source: We also detected HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc on the exoskeleton, with estimated release rates of 3–6 ng/hr and larvae (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MBOA-Glc was predominant in the frass at an average concentration of 11.4 mg*g FM−1.
source: MBOA-Glc was predominant in the frass, at an average concentration of 11.4 mg*g FM−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 1B.

claim: The concentration of sequestered HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc varied between experiments, suggesting a possible impact of environmental conditions and/or small differences in larval age on sequestration patterns.
source: Interestingly, the concentration of sequestered HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc varied between experiments, suggesting a possible impact of environmental conditions and/or small differences in larval age on sequestration patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observed variation in the data.

claim: Most larval BX levels mirror plant BX levels, with the exception of HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc.
source: A comparison of BX concentrations in maize roots and D. virgifera larvae that fed on these roots from hatching until third instar revealed that most larval BX levels mirror plant BX levels, with the exception of HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Although BX abundance in D. virgifera larvae were reduced by approximately 95% compared to plants, HDMBOA-Glc levels were reduced by only 50%.
source: Although the BX abundance in the larvae were reduced by approximately 95%, HDMBOA-Glc levels were reduced by only 50% and MBOA-Glc was exclusively found in D. virgifera (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MBOA-Glc was exclusively found in D. virgifera larvae and not in the plants.
source: Although the BX abundance in the larvae were reduced by approximately 95%, HDMBOA-Glc levels were reduced by only 50% and MBOA-Glc was exclusively found in D. virgifera (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Feeding D. virgifera larvae on BX-free igl bx1 double mutant plants led to the complete absence of BXs in the larvae, including MBOA-Glc.
source: Feeding D. virgifera larvae on BX-free igl bx1 double mutant plants (Ahmad et al., 2011) led to the complete absence of BXs in the larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), including MBOA-Glc, demonstrating that BXs in D. virgifera are plant-derived.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BXs in D. virgifera are plant-derived.
source: Feeding D. virgifera larvae on BX-free igl bx1 double mutant plants (Ahmad et al., 2011) led to the complete absence of BXs in the larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), including MBOA-Glc, demonstrating that BXs in D. virgifera are plant-derived.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing absence of BXs in larvae fed on BX-free plants.

claim: Feeding on bx1 mutant plants which show a 90% reduction in BX levels still resulted in significant accumulation of HDMBOA-Glc in D. virgifera larvae.
source: By contrast, feeding on bx1 mutant plants which show a 90% reduction in BX levels (Maag et al., 2016) still resulted in a significant, albeit lower accumulation of HDMBOA-Glc in D. virgifera larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation about bx1 mutant characteristics.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc release from the exoskeleton did not differ between wild type B73 and bx1 mutant fed larvae.
source: HDMBOA-Glc release from the exoskeleton did not differ between wild type (WT) B73 and bx1 mutant fed larvae, while MBOA-Glc release was significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: MBOA-Glc release from the exoskeleton was significantly reduced in bx1 mutant fed larvae compared to WT B73 fed larvae.
source: HDMBOA-Glc release from the exoskeleton did not differ between wild type (WT) B73 and bx1 mutant fed larvae, while MBOA-Glc release was significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observed accumulation patterns suggest a high degree of structural selectivity regarding uptake and sequestration of BXs by D. virgifera.
source: The observed accumulation patterns suggest a high degree of structural selectivity regarding uptake and sequestration of BXs by D. virgifera.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing differential accumulation of different BX compounds.

claim: MBOA is a benzoxazolinone-type BX that is a common product of DIMBOA and HDMBOA degradation in insect guts.
source: MBOA, a benzoxazolinone-type BX, is a common product of DIMBOA and HDMBOA degradation in insect guts that has negative consequences for insect herbivores (Wouters et al., 2016; Glauser et al., 2011; Maag et al., 2014; Wouters et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MBOA has negative consequences for insect herbivores.
source: MBOA, a benzoxazolinone-type BX, is a common product of DIMBOA and HDMBOA degradation in insect guts that has negative consequences for insect herbivores (Wouters et al., 2016; Glauser et al., 2011; Maag et al., 2014; Wouters et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When D. virgifera gut extracts were incubated with MBOA, MBOA-Glc was readily formed.
source: When D. virgifera gut extracts were incubated with MBOA, MBOA-Glc was readily formed (Figure 2A), suggesting that D. virgifera is capable of this N-glycosylation reaction as leaf feeding caterpillars are (Maag et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: D. virgifera is capable of N-glycosylation of MBOA as leaf feeding caterpillars are.
source: When D. virgifera gut extracts were incubated with MBOA, MBOA-Glc was readily formed (Figure 2A), suggesting that D. virgifera is capable of this N-glycosylation reaction as leaf feeding caterpillars are (Maag et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and comparison to cited literature on leaf feeding caterpillars.

claim: MBOA-Glc was not deglycosylated by a root extract.
source: Since MBOA-Glc was not deglycosylated by a root extract (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it may represent a stable form of BX that can be absorbed from the gut by D. virgifera without toxic consequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MBOA-Glc may represent a stable form of BX that can be absorbed from the gut by D. virgifera without toxic consequences.
source: Since MBOA-Glc was not deglycosylated by a root extract (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it may represent a stable form of BX that can be absorbed from the gut by D. virgifera without toxic consequences.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data showing MBOA-Glc stability.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc is rapidly hydrolyzed by plant-derived β-glucosidases.
source: In contrast to MBOA-Glc, HDMBOA-Glc is a common plant BX that is rapidly hydrolyzed by plant-derived β-glucosidases (Glauser et al., 2011), and the resulting aglycone is highly unstable (Nishida, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aglycone resulting from HDMBOA-Glc hydrolysis is highly unstable.
source: In contrast to MBOA-Glc, HDMBOA-Glc is a common plant BX that is rapidly hydrolyzed by plant-derived β-glucosidases (Glauser et al., 2011), and the resulting aglycone is highly unstable (Nishida, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No other maize-feeding herbivore apart from D. virgifera is known to be able to accumulate HDMBOA-Glc.
source: To date, no other maize-feeding herbivore apart from D. virgifera is known to be able to accumulate HDMBOA-Glc (Wouters et al., 2016; Glauser et al., 2011; Maag et al., 2014; Wouters et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc was hydrolyzed in D. virgifera gut extracts both in presence and absence of added β-glucosidase.
source: HDMBOA-Glc was hydrolyzed both in presence and absence of the gut extracts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No [13C]-labeled HDMBOA-Glc was detected when gut extracts were incubated with HDMBOA-Glc, β-glucosidase, and [13C6] UDP-glucose within 3 hr.
source: To determine if D. virgifera can reglycosylate free HDMBOA, we incubated gut extracts with HDMBOA-Glc, β-glucosidase, and [13C6] UDP-glucose and analyzed aliquots of the extracts over time (5, 60, 180 min). No [13C]-labeled HDMBOA-Glc was detected within the 3 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the isotope labeling experiment.

claim: In vitro experiments suggest that HDMBOA-Glc accumulation does not proceed via inhibition of HDMBOA-Glc hydrolysis in the D. virgifera gut nor by reglycosylation of free HDMBOA.
source: Thus, our in vitro experiments suggest that HDMBOA-Glc accumulation does not proceed via inhibition of HDMBOA-Glc hydrolysis in the D. virgifera gut nor by reglycosylation of free HDMBOA.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing hydrolysis and lack of reglycosylation.

claim: Alternative strategies for HDMBOA-Glc accumulation in the hemolymph may include rapid transport or transient stabilization through other chemical modifications.
source: Alternative strategies for HDMBOA-Glc accumulation in the hemolymph may include rapid transport (Abdalsamee et al., 2014) or transient stabilization through other chemical modifications (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to possible mechanisms from the literature.

claim: When D. virgifera larvae were crushed with forceps, HDMBOA-Glc was rapidly broken down and MBOA accumulated at concentrations of >25 µg/g FM.
source: When we simulated predator attack by crushing the larvae with forceps, HDMBOA-Glc was rapidly broken down, and the final catabolite MBOA (Maresh et al., 2006) accumulated at concentrations of >25 µg/g FM (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation about MBOA as a catabolite.

claim: No reduction in MBOA-Glc levels was observed when D. virgifera larvae were crushed.
source: No reduction in MBOA-Glc levels was observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When D. virgifera larvae were exposed to the EPN Heterorhabditis bacteriophora, MBOA concentrations increased.
source: When D. virgifera larvae were exposed to the EPN Heterorhabditis bacteriophora, MBOA concentrations increased as well, albeit at lower levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: D. virgifera produces MBOA via HDMBOA-Glc degradation upon predator and EPN attack.
source: Together, these results show that D. virgifera produces MBOA via HDMBOA-Glc degradation upon predator and EPN attack.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing MBOA production upon mechanical disruption and EPN exposure.

claim: Heterorhabditis bacteriophora infective juveniles degraded HDMBOA-Glc to MBOA.
source: Heterorhabditis bacteriophora infective juveniles degraded HDMBOA-Glc to MBOA (Figure 2E), but not MBOA-Glc.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Heterorhabditis bacteriophora infective juveniles did not degrade MBOA-Glc.
source: Heterorhabditis bacteriophora infective juveniles degraded HDMBOA-Glc to MBOA (Figure 2E), but not MBOA-Glc.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MBOA was not further converted by H. bacteriophora.
source: MBOA was not further converted by H. bacteriophora (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The entomopathogenic bacterium Photorhabdus luminescens catabolized both HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc, albeit at very low efficiency.
source: The entomopathogenic bacterium, Photorhabdus luminescens, a symbiont of H. bacteriophora, catabolized both HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA-Glc, albeit at very low efficiency (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The activation of sequestered plant toxins may occur upon contact with predator-derived factors.
source: This work shows that the activation of sequestered plant toxins may occur upon contact with predator-derived factors, which may represent an additional route by which stabilized plant toxins can be used as anti-predator defenses by herbivores.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the experimental data showing BX activation by EPNs.

claim: Infectivity by EPNs was around 15% on WT-fed D. virgifera.
source: Infectivity by EPNs was around 15% on WT-fed D. virgifera.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 3A.

claim: On bx1-fed D. virgifera, EPN infectivity increased to 40%.
source: On bx1-fed D. virgifera, infectivity increased to 40% (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT-fed D. virgifera are significantly more resistant to EPNs than larvae fed on BX-deficient bx1 and bx2 mutants in the W22 genetic background.
source: Experiments with BX-deficient bx1 and bx2 mutants in the genetic background W22 (Tzin et al., 2015) confirmed that WT-fed D. virgifera are significantly more resistant to EPNs than larvae fed on BX-deficient mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and a citation about the mutants.

claim: At physiological doses, pre-exposure to HDMBOA-Glc suppressed H. bacteriophora infectivity toward D. balteata by 50%.
source: At physiological doses, pre-exposure to HDMBOA-Glc suppressed H. bacteriophora infectivity toward the non-sequestering D. balteata by 50% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MBOA-Glc and MBOA pre-exposure did not have any significant effect on H. bacteriophora infectivity toward D. balteata.
source: MBOA-Glc and MBOA pre-exposure did not have any significant effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 3B.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc increased H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro by 10%.
source: HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA increased H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro by 10% and 20%, while MBOA-Glc had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MBOA increased H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro by 20%.
source: HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA increased H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro by 10% and 20%, while MBOA-Glc had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MBOA-Glc had no significant effect on H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro.
source: HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA increased H. bacteriophora mortality in vitro by 10% and 20%, while MBOA-Glc had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photorhabdus luminescens growth was inhibited by MBOA starting at concentrations of 25 µg/g.
source: Photorhabdus luminescens growth was inhibited by MBOA starting at concentrations of 25 µg/g and HDMBOA-Glc starting at concentrations of 100 µg/g (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photorhabdus luminescens growth was inhibited by HDMBOA-Glc starting at concentrations of 100 µg/g.
source: Photorhabdus luminescens growth was inhibited by MBOA starting at concentrations of 25 µg/g and HDMBOA-Glc starting at concentrations of 100 µg/g (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MBOA-Glc did not have any effect on Photorhabdus luminescens growth.
source: Again, MBOA-Glc did not have any effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 3D.

claim: BX-dependent resistance of D. virgifera against EPNs is associated with strong toxicity of HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA against both the nematode and its endobiontic bacterium.
source: These experiments show that BX-dependent resistance of D. virgifera against EPNs is associated with strong toxicity of HDMBOA-Glc and MBOA against both the nematode and its endobiontic bacterium.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing effects on both nematodes and bacteria.

claim: Sequestered and reactivated BXs protect D. virgifera against predation by the third and the fourth trophic levels.
source: Together with the mutant experiments, these data show that sequestered and reactivated BXs protect D. virgifera against predation by the third and the fourth trophic levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined experimental data on nematodes and bacteria.

claim: BXs accumulate on the exoskeleton of D. virgifera.
source: As BXs also accumulate on the exoskeleton of D. virgifera (Figure 1B), we hypothesized that they may interfere with EPN host location and preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: H. bacteriophora infective juveniles were significantly more attracted to bx1-fed D. virgifera larvae than larvae fed on WT plants.
source: In choice tests, H. bacteriophora infective juveniles were significantly more attracted to bx1-fed D. virgifera larvae than larvae fed on WT plants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H. bacteriophora were more attracted to aqueous surface extracts of bx1-fed larvae compared to WT-fed larvae.
source: The same pattern was found when aqueous surface extracts of bx1- and WT-fed larvae were compared (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Complementing surface extracts of BX-free D. virgifera with MBOA-Glc at physiological doses significantly reduced their attractiveness for H. bacteriophora.
source: Complementing surface extracts of BX-free D. virgifera with MBOA-Glc or a mixture of MBOA-Glc and HDMBOA-Glc at physiological doses significantly reduced their attractiveness for H. bacteriophora (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Complementing surface extracts of BX-free D. virgifera with a mixture of MBOA-Glc and HDMBOA-Glc at physiological doses significantly reduced their attractiveness for H. bacteriophora.
source: Complementing surface extracts of BX-free D. virgifera with MBOA-Glc or a mixture of MBOA-Glc and HDMBOA-Glc at physiological doses significantly reduced their attractiveness for H. bacteriophora (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc alone had no effect on EPN attraction.
source: HDMBOA-Glc alone had no effect on EPN attraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 4B.

claim: MBOA-Glc reduces the attractiveness of D. virgifera to EPNs.
source: Thus, MBOA-Glc reduces the attractiveness of D. virgifera to EPNs.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing reduced attraction with MBOA-Glc.

claim: D. virgifera stores BXs, which it stabilizes and re-activates to disrupt EPN infection at different levels.
source: Together, the results above show that D. virgifera stores BXs, which it stabilizes and re-activates to disrupt EPN infection at different levels (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary inference from all the experimental data presented.

claim: MBOA-Glc is released in the frass and on the exoskeleton as a repellent for host-searching infective juvenile nematodes.
source: First, the relatively stable MBOA-Glc is released in the frass and on the exoskeleton as a repellent for host-searching infective juvenile nematodes.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing MBOA-Glc in frass/exoskeleton and its repellent effects.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc is activated to produce MBOA, which reduces the growth of the symbiotic bacteria injected into the haemocoel by EPNs.
source: Second, HDMBOA-Glc is activated to produce MBOA, which reduces the growth of the symbiotic bacteria injected into the haemocoel by EPNs to kill and pre-digest the larvae.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing HDMBOA-Glc activation and MBOA effects on bacteria.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc and its reactivation products kill EPNs directly and thereby likely reduce the infectiveness of the next generation of emerging infective juveniles.
source: Third, HDMBOA-Glc and its reactivation products kill EPNs directly and thereby likely reduce the infectiveness of the next generation of emerging infective juveniles.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the experimental data showing EPN mortality.

claim: By interfering with different processes, D. virgifera larvae become highly resistant to EPNs.
source: By interfering with these different processes, D. virgifera larvae become highly resistant to EPNs.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined experimental data showing multiple mechanisms of resistance.

claim: D. virgifera larvae are gregarious, and larvae from the same batch of eggs often feed together on the same host plant.
source: D. virgifera larvae are gregarious, and larvae from the same batch of eggs often feed together on the same host plant (Robert et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Reducing the build-up of high EPN densities within the rhizosphere may protect siblings from infection.
source: Reducing the build-up of high EPN densities within the rhizosphere may therefore also protect siblings from infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the gregarious behavior and the observed effects on EPNs.

claim: Storing plant toxins for self-defense may be particularly advantageous, as it allows herbivores to escape bottom-up and top-down controls at the same time.
source: Storing plant toxins for self-defense may be particularly advantageous, as it allows herbivores to escape bottom-up and top-down controls at the same time (Kumar et al., 2014; Erb and Robert, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A specialized and highly destructive maize pest has evolved the ability to utilize the major toxins of its host plant to escape predation by soil-borne natural enemies.
source: Our work illustrates how a specialized and highly destructive maize pest has evolved the ability to utilize the major toxins of its host plant to escape predation by soil-borne natural enemies.
evidence: This is an inference from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The protective effect of BX sequestration is achieved through selective stabilization and reactivation of the toxins.
source: This protective effect is achieved through selective stabilization and reactivation of the toxins, which allows the herbivore to target different stages of the infection process of entomopathogenic nematodes and their endobiotic bacteria and thereby suppresses infection rates by over 50%.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing the mechanisms and their effects.

claim: BX sequestration allows D. virgifera to target different stages of the infection process of entomopathogenic nematodes and their endobiotic bacteria and thereby suppresses infection rates by over 50%.
source: This protective effect is achieved through selective stabilization and reactivation of the toxins, which allows the herbivore to target different stages of the infection process of entomopathogenic nematodes and their endobiotic bacteria and thereby suppresses infection rates by over 50%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced infection rates in WT-fed versus mutant-fed larvae.

claim: These results advance our basic understanding on the impact of plant chemistry on trophic cascades.
source: These results advance our basic understanding on the impact of plant chemistry on trophic cascades and provide an explanation for the limited success of biological control programs targeting the western corn rootworm (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: These results provide an explanation for the limited success of biological control programs targeting the western corn rootworm.
source: These results advance our basic understanding on the impact of plant chemistry on trophic cascades and provide an explanation for the limited success of biological control programs targeting the western corn rootworm (Gray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data combined with cited knowledge about biological control programs.
